# The Line and What It Is For

## A Line Is the Simplest Conditional Expectation

**The goal of this section:** say what a line drawn through a scatter of
people is actually claiming.

Last week's conditional expectation function could be any shape. A line
commits to the simplest one there is: whatever schooling you have, your
expected earnings move by the same amount for one more year.

::: {.defn title="What we want from it"}
Given a person's years of schooling and nothing else, what is our best guess
of their hourly earnings?
:::

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

## The Simple Regression Model and Its Notation

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_i - 12) + u_i
\end{equation}
```

- $y_i$: hourly earnings of person $i$, in euro
- $x_i$: years of schooling of person $i$
- $\beta_0$: expected earnings at twelve years of schooling
- $\beta_1$: the change in expected earnings for one more year
- $u_i$: everything else that moves person $i$'s earnings

::: {.caveat title="Why subtract twelve"}
Without it, $\beta_0$ would be expected earnings for a person with no
schooling at all, and nobody in this population has that. Centring buys a
constant you can read out loud.
:::

## Hat Notation: Population Parameter Versus Sample Estimate

::: {.defn title="The convention, once, before any algebra"}
$\beta_1$ is the number in the population. We will never see it.
$\hat{\beta}_1$ is what we compute from a sample. It is a different object,
it changes every time we draw a new sample, and the whole of week 6 is about
the relationship between the two.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Watch for this in your own writing. A sentence containing $\beta_1$ is a claim
about the world; a sentence containing $\hat{\beta}_1$ is a claim about your
data.
:::

## Vote: What Are the Units of the Slope?

Earnings are in euro per hour. Schooling is in years.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what would a slope of
$-0.4$ mean, in a sentence with no symbols in it?
:::

# Least Squares

## Comparing Candidate Lines Through the Same Scatter

**The goal of this section:** choose one line out of all the lines we could
draw, and be honest that it is a choice.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-1_candidates.png}{Three lines through the same 120
people. The sum of squared residuals is printed beside each.}
```

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## The Least-Squares Criterion

For any candidate line, every person has a **residual**: the gap between
what they earn and what the line says they earn.

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{SSR}(b_0, b_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}
  \bigl(y_i - b_0 - b_1 (x_i - 12)\bigr)^2
\end{equation}
```

- $b_0, b_1$: any candidate pair, not yet the chosen ones
- $\mathrm{SSR}$: the total of the squared gaps

::: {.result}
Least squares is the pair that makes this number as small as possible. That
is the entire definition. It is a criterion someone chose, not a law.
:::

## Residuals as Vertical Distances From the Fitted Line

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-1_residuals.png}{The fitted line and all 120
residuals. Least squares makes the total of their squares as small as it can
be.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
The segments are the figure. A scatter with a line through it hides the thing
least squares is actually about.
:::

## Vote: Why Squares and Not Absolute Values?

We could have minimised the total absolute gap instead.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: what does squaring do to one person who is very
far from the line?
:::

# Reading the Slope

## The Slope Is Euro Per Year

**The goal of this section:** say what the number means in the units the data
came in, and then say what it does not mean.

::: {.worked title="Reading this estimate out loud"}
Comparing two people whose schooling differs by one year, the one with more
schooling earns about $\hat{\beta}_1$ euro more per hour, on average, in this
sample.
:::

::: {.caveat}
Notice what that sentence does not say. It does not say that giving a person
another year of school would raise their pay by that amount. Nothing we have
done today licenses that, and week 12 is about why.
:::

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## How a Few High Earners Shift the Fitted Line

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-1_leverage.png}{The same population with a handful
of very high earners switched on. Green is the line without them, dashed navy
the line with.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Squaring the residuals is what does this. One person a long way from the line
contributes more to the SSR than twenty people close to it, so the line moves
to accommodate them.
:::

## Vote: Should We Drop the Highest Earners?

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: what would you need to know about those people
before you could answer?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: the line fits whether or not schooling causes
earnings. Least squares has no opinion on the matter, and neither does the
R output.]

## Summary: The Three Ideas in Today's Lecture

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **The Line and What It Is For.** A line is the simplest conditional expectation there is.
2. **Least Squares.** Least squares is a criterion, and someone chose it.
3. **Reading the Slope.** The slope is a rate, in euro per year, and it is fragile.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: how much of the variation that line actually accounts for, and why that is a smaller claim than it sounds.
:::

## Derivation: The Least-Squares Estimators

Minimise the sum of squared residuals with respect to the two unknowns, set
both derivatives to zero, and solve the pair.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Differentiate, set to zero, solve. The step that does the work is
the second: setting the derivative to zero is what makes the residuals sum to
zero and be uncorrelated with schooling, and those two facts are what every
result in weeks 5 and 6 rests on.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
